headline: Shell’s Arc Deal Helps Lift Foreign Investment in Canada to Two-Year High
author: Erik Hertzberg

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Foreign direct investment in Canada rose to its highest quarterly level in more than two years, driven by outlays into the country's energy and mining sectors.

FDI totaled C$33.7 billion ($23.7 billion) in the third quarter, up from C$29.8 billion in the second quarter, according to data released Friday by Statistics Canada. The increase was driven by mergers and acquisitions, as well as earnings "reinvested in Canadian affiliates by their foreign parents," the agency said.

More than half of the foreign direct investment was in the energy and mining sector, with the UK and US accounting for most of the inflows. FDI from the UK was the highest in nearly two decades. Canadian direct investment abroad totaled C$31.5 billion, up from C$20.2 billion previously.
UK-headquartered Shell PLC completed its acquisition of ARC Resources Ltd., an energy company with operations in Alberta and British Columbia, during the quarter.
The data offer an early benchmark for Prime Minister Mark Carney's push to attract more capital to Canada, though most of the quarter likely predates his government's biggest investment incentives.

Carney has set a goal of "catalyzing" C$1 trillion in investment over five years. In September, he hosted some of the world's biggest money managers in Toronto for the inaugural Canada Investment Summit, where the government pitched dozens of firms on possible stakes in Canadian natural resources, manufacturing and other projects.

His government has also made the most significant changes in decades to the tax treatment of business investments. The "productivity mega deduction," announced at the summit in September, allows firms to immediately expense a broad range of capital investments.

The measure carries a C$36 billion price tag over half a decade, and is part of a shift in fiscal policy that Carney and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne say is aimed at sparking an "investment super-cycle."

Shelly Kaushik, an economist with the Bank of Montreal, said the data is "starting to show signs of the tide turning on the attractiveness of doing business in Canada." She added that it's still early, and Carney's latest initiatives have yet to show up in the numbers.
The release shows Canada's current account surplus narrowed to C$4.5 billion, from C$6.1 billion previously.
